articles.title: SBOM Minimum Elements in Practice: What Breaks After the First Release
articles.excerpt: SBOM Minimum Elements in Practice: What Breaks After the First Release Software bills of materials (SBOMs) moved from a niche supply-chain practice to a procurement expectation. Generating one is no l…
articles.body: SBOM Minimum Elements in Practice: What Breaks After the First Release Software bills of materials (SBOMs) moved from a niche supply-chain practice to a procurement expectation. Generating one is no longer the hard part. Keeping them accurate enough to answer a question during an incident is. The commonly cited baseline comes from the minimum-elements work that fed into NIST guidance on software supply-chain security, and the fields are unglamorous: supplier name, component name, component version, other unique identifiers, dependency relationship, author of the SBOM data, and a timestamp. Formats such as SPDX and CycloneDX carry those fields. The operational failure modes show up later.

articles.title: Free MiniMax, zero API keys: build a read-only SQL report app
articles.excerpt: Vercel is serving MiniMax M3.1 Flash for free until 22 October [2]. Free model, short window. So obviously we built something with it. 🛠️ The idea is simple. Let the model write SQL. Never let it run…
articles.body: Vercel is serving MiniMax M3.1 Flash for free until 22 October [2]. Free model, short window. So obviously we built something with it. 🛠️ The idea is simple. Let the model write SQL. Never let it run SQL. A small local app takes the query, runs it on read-only sample data, and shows you the report. If the query tries anything funny, SQLite says no. No API key. No signup beyond your Vercel account. About ten minutes. The finished app running a query MiniMax actually wrote. Sample data is made up: twelve fake orders. What we're building Meet SQL Postcard . Two boxes: Generate: you copy a prompt into Vercel's MiniMax playground and get SQL back. Check & run: you paste that SQL into the app. It runs on a fresh in-memory SQLite database with twelve fake orders.

articles.title: 500 Async Calls, One Number That Explains Why
articles.excerpt: I shipped a background job that fanned out to a downstream API for every row in a batch, wrapped the whole thing in Task.WhenAll, and watched it work beautifully in testing. Then someone ran it agains…
articles.body: I shipped a background job that fanned out to a downstream API for every row in a batch, wrapped the whole thing in Task.WhenAll , and watched it work beautifully in testing. Then someone ran it against a real batch of a few hundred rows and the downstream service started returning timeouts. Nothing in my code was slow. I'd just asked it to make every single call at the exact same instant, and the thing on the other end wasn't built for that. The fix was one method. But before I changed anything I wanted a number that showed me what was actually happening, because "it felt like too much load" isn't something I can put in a PR description. Measuring the thing nobody measures Load is easy to hand-wave about and hard to see.

articles.body: WordPress has moved fast this year. Version 7.0 arrived on May 20 and 7.1 followed on August 19, so if you look after client sites, here is a plain summary of what matters. AI in core, on your terms. 7.0 added a provider agnostic AI client and a Connectors screen, so plugins can talk to AI services through one standard setup. API keys for providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are supported. It's all optional, and a good habit is to treat anything it writes, like titles or alt text, as a first draft. Responsive styling without custom CSS. In 7.1 you can set block styles per viewport (tablet and mobile) in the Site Editor, and developers can define custom breakpoints in theme.json . Hover, focus and active states start with the Button block.

articles.title: Web developers should stand against thoughtlessness
articles.excerpt: Seventeen years ago, web developers developed responsive components with lots of hacking because they thought that the user interface and the content did not change. They followed design mockups witho…
articles.body: Seventeen years ago, web developers developed responsive components with lots of hacking because they thought that the user interface and the content did not change. They followed design mockups without thinking about how people would use their websites. Now you have all the necessary CSS properties to develop responsive components for all devices and all mainstream browsers. You have everything. But you are not ready to think about how people would use your website if you still write code to match your website with a design file, such as Figma and Sketch files. No matter how many new and awesome CSS properties are brought to you, you can not build responsive components. You can not develop responsive layouts. You can not serve responsive websites to all your users. You must change.

An Anticrepuscular Rainbow Fan Explanation: This is an unusual rainbow. For one thing, the rainbow is not complete, appearing only in a sunlit fan — but that by itself is not very unusual. articles.title: 8 Classic PlayStation Adventure Games that are Barely Playable Today
articles.excerpt: From Tomb Raider to Silent Hill, eight classic PlayStation games whose tank controls, cameras, or lost code make them hard to play today
articles.body: If you’ve ever watched someone play an old PlayStation game and wondered why their character keeps spinning around in circles, congratulations, you’ve already met tank controls. If you’re unfamiliar, here’s your quick introduction: With tank controls, pressing up moves your character forward in whatever direction they’re facing, and pressing left or right only rotates them, so with the stick alone, you can’t sidestep or turn on a dime. That’s manageable in a hallway. It’s much less so when you’re sneaking past a guard, lining up a shot, or timing a leap across a pit, which is why the same scheme caused trouble in just about every genre during the PS1 era. These eight classic games are the hardest to go back to, whether the culprit is tank controls or something else entirely.

articles.body: Millennials get a lot of flak for being overly nostalgic, but I don't think that's fair. When the modern-day world has nothing to offer us but AI slop, shrinkflation and a sad acceptance that we can't be bothered to do anything about global warming. It's easy to see why we yearn for the days of Pogs, the Backstreet Boys, and Saved by the Bell. One area that we definitely had it good in the 90s was sci-fi , when legendary shows like Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stargate SG-1, and — of course — The X-Files ruled our TV screens long before the age of streaming services . You can relive those glory days of alien conspiracies, spooky happenings and cell phones the size of a brick with the Lego Ideas The X-Files set.

articles.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
articles.excerpt: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment remini…
articles.body: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.
